name: GO 2023 Topic Wise Free Test 2 | First Order Logic

question.text:
If $Mr.M$ is guilty, then no witness is lying unless he is afraid. There is a witness who is afraid. Which of the following statements is true?

(Hint: Formulate the problem using the following predicates

  • $G - Mr.M$ is guilty
  • $W(x) - x$ is a witness
  • $L(x) - x$ is lying
  • $A(x) - x$ is afraid )
  1. $Mr.M$ is guilty.
  2. $Mr.M$ is not guilty.
  3. From these facts one cannot conclude that $Mr.M$ is guilty.
  4. There is a witness who is lying.

Consider the following argument with premise $\forall _x (\text{P}(x) \vee \text{Q}(x))$ and conclusion $(\forall _x \text{P}(x)) \wedge (\forall _x \text{Q}(x))$

$$\begin{array}{|ll|l|} \hline \text{(A)} & \forall _x (\text{P}(x) \vee \text{Q}(x)) & \text{Premise} \\ \hline \text{(B)} & \text{P}(c) \vee \text{Q}(c) & \text{Universal instantiation from (A)} \\ \hline \text{(C)} & \text{P}(c) & \text{Simplification from (B)} \\ \hline \text{(D)} & \forall _x \text{P}(x) & \text{Universal Generalization of (C)} \\ \hline \text{(E)} & \text{Q}(c) & \text{Simplification from (B)} \\ \hline \text{(F}) & \forall _x \text{Q}(x) & \text{Universal Generalization of (E)} \\ \hline \text{(G}) & (\forall _x \text{P}(x)) \wedge (\forall _x\text{Q}(x)) & \text{Conjuction of (D) and (F)} \\ \hline \end{array}$$

  1. This is a valid argument
  2. Steps $\text{(C)}$ and $\text{(E)}$ are not correct inferences
  3. Steps $\text{(D)}$ and $\text{(F)}$ are not correct inferences
  4. Step $\text{(G)}$ is not a correct inference

Which of the following propositional formulas is a tautology?
  1. $p \rightarrow(q \rightarrow p).$
  2. $p.$
  3. $p \vee p.$
  4. $(p \rightarrow q) \wedge(q \rightarrow p).$

Consider the following predicates:

  • $\operatorname{bird}(x): x$ is a bird.
  • $\text{penguin} (x): x$ is a penguin.
  • $\text{fly} (x) : x$ can fly.

Consider the following predicate logic expressions:

  1. $\forall x .[(\operatorname{bird}(x) \wedge \neg$ penguin $(x)) \rightarrow$ fly $(x)]$
  2. bird(Tweety) $\wedge \neg$ fly(Tweety)

Which of the following is implied by $\mathrm{A}, \mathrm{B}?$

  1. penguin(Tweety)
  2. $\neg$ penguin(Tweety)
  3. Tweety is a penguin or not, can not be determined.
  4. fly(Tweety)

Which of the following formulas does not express that there is exactly one element of $\text{D}$ that has property $\text{P}(x)?$

  1. $\exists x \in \text{D} \forall y \in \text{D}[\text{P}(y) \leftrightarrow y=x]$
  2. $\exists x \in \text{D}[\text{P}(x) \wedge \forall y \in \text{D}[y \neq x \rightarrow \neg \text{P}(y)]]$
  3. $\exists x \in \text{D} \text{P}(x) \wedge \forall x_1, x_2 \in \text{D}\left[\text{P}\left(x_1\right) \wedge \text{P}\left(x_2\right) \rightarrow x_1=x_2\right]$
  4. $\exists x \in \text{D} \forall y \in \text{D}[\text{P}(y) \rightarrow y=x]$

For a person $p$, let $w(p)$, $A(p, y)$, $L(p)$ and $J(p)$ denote that $p$ is a woman, $p$ admires $y$, $p$ is a lawyer and $p$ is a judge respectively. Which of the following is the correct translation in first order logic of the sentence: "All woman who are lawyers admire some judge"?

  1. $\forall x: \left[\left(w\left(x\right)\Lambda L \left(x\right)\right)\Rightarrow \left(\exists y:\left(J \left(y\right)\Lambda w\left(y\right) \Lambda A\left(x, y\right)\right)\right)\right]$
  2. $\forall x: \left[\left(w\left(x\right)\Rightarrow L \left(x\right)\right)\Rightarrow \left(\exists y:\left(J \left(y\right) \Lambda A\left(x, y\right)\right)\right)\right]$
  3. $\exists y \forall x: \left[\left(w\left(x\right) \Lambda L\left(x\right)\right) \Rightarrow \left(J\left(y\right) \Lambda A\left(x, y\right)\right)\right]$
  4. $\forall x: \left[\left(w\left(x\right) \Lambda L\left(x\right)\right) \Rightarrow \left(\exists y: \left(J\left(y\right) \Lambda A\left(x, y\right)\right)\right)\right]$

Consider the following English sentence:

$\text{“Agra and Gwalior are both in India"}.$

A student has written a logical sentence for the above English sentence in First-Order Logic using predicate $\text{IN}(x, y),$ which means $x$ is in $y,$ as follows.

$\text{In(Agra, India)} \vee \text{In(Gwalior, India)}$

Which one of the following is correct with respect to the above logical sentence?

  1. It is syntactically valid but does not express the meaning of the English sentence
  2. It is syntactically valid and expresses the meaning of the English sentence also
  3. It is syntactically invalid but expresses the meaning of the English sentence
  4. It is syntactically invalid and does not express the meaning of the English sentence

Consider the following predicates:

  • $\operatorname{bird}(x): x$ is a bird.
  • $ ext{penguin}(x): x$ is a penguin.
  • $ ext{fly} (x): x$ can fly.

Consider the following sentence:

All birds except penguins' fly. (Note that Penguins may or may not fly)

Which of the following is/are a formula in first-order logic expressing the given fact?

  1. $ orall x.[(\operatorname{bird}(x) \wedge eg$ penguin $(x)) ightarrow \mathrm{fly}(x)]$
  2. $ orall x.[ eg \operatorname{bird}(x) \vee eg$ penguin $(x) \vee$ fly $(x)]$
  3. $ orall x. [ eg$ bird $(x) \vee$ penguin $(x) \vee$ fly $(x)]$
  4. $ orall x. [\operatorname{bird}(x) \vee$ penguin $(x) \vee$ fly $(x)]$

Which of the following is a valid inference of $\mathrm{X, Y}$ in first-order logic?
$$
\begin{aligned}
& \text{X}: \forall x .(\mathrm{P}(x) \rightarrow \mathrm{Q}(x)) \\
& \text {Y}: \forall x .(\neg \mathrm{R}(x) \rightarrow \neg \mathrm{Q}(x))
\end{aligned}
$$

  1. $\forall x .(\neg \text{R}(x) \rightarrow \neg \text{P}(x))$
  2. $\forall x .(\mathrm{P}(x) \rightarrow \mathrm{R}(x))$
  3. $\forall x .(\mathrm{R}(x) \rightarrow \mathrm{P}(x))$
  4. $\forall x .(\mathrm{Q}(x) \rightarrow \mathrm{R}(x))$

Which of the following is NOT necessarily true? { Notation: The symbol ''$\neg$''notes negation; $\text{P} (x, y)$ means that for given $x$ and $y$, the property $\text{P}(x, y)$ is true }.

  1. $(\forall x\forall y \text{P}(x, y)) \Rightarrow (\forall y\forall x \text{P}(x, y))$
  2. $(\exists x\exists y \text{P}(x, y)) \Rightarrow  (\exists y\exists x \text{P}(x, y))$
  3. $(\exists x\forall y \text{P}(x, y)) \Rightarrow  (\forall y\exists x \text{P}(x, y))$
  4. $(\forall x\exists y \text{P}(x, y)) \Rightarrow  (\exists y\forall x \text{P}(x, y))$

In first-order logic, how would you express that "something likes something"?
  1. $\exists x \exists y \operatorname{Likes}(x, y)$
  2. $\exists x \forall y \operatorname{Likes}(x, \mathrm{y})$
  3. $\forall x \exists y \text{Likes}(x, y)$
  4. $\forall x \forall y \operatorname{Likes}(x, \mathrm{y})$

Let $\varphi$ be a propositional formula on a set of variables  $A$ and  $\psi$ be a propositional  formula on a set of  variables $B$ , such that $\varphi$ $\Rightarrow$ $\psi$ . A $\textit{Craig interpolant}$ of $\varphi$ and $\psi$ is a propositional formula $\mu$ on variables $A \cap B$ such that $\varphi$ $\Rightarrow$ $\mu$ and $\mu$ $\Rightarrow$ $\psi$. Given propositional formula $\varphi = q \vee (r \wedge s)$ on the set of variables $A = \{q,r,s\}$ and propositional formula $\psi = \neg q \rightarrow (s \vee t)$ on the set of variables $B =\{q,s,t\}$, which of the following is a Craig interpolant for $\varphi$ and $\psi?$ 

  1. $\varphi$ itself
  2. $q \vee s$
  3. $q \vee r$
  4. $\neg q \wedge s$

Given that

  • $B(x)$ means "$x$ is a bat",
  • $F(x)$ means "$x$ is a fly", and
  • $E(x, y)$ means "$x$ eats $y$",

what is the best English translation of $$ \forall x(F(x) \rightarrow \forall y (E(y, x) \rightarrow B(y)))?$$

  1. all flies eat bats
  2. bats eat only flies
  3. every bat eats flies
  4. only bats eat flies
